Chapter Five: The Foundation of Morality and the Search for Meaning
Every day, we make choices that show what we really value—sometimes without even realizing it. Imagine a business owner who’s tempted to cut corners, but decides to do the right thing, even when nobody’s watching. Or a teenager, feeling the pressure to fit in, but still stands up for a friend who’s being bullied. And then there’s the nurse, totally exhausted after a long shift, who somehow finds the strength to care for one more patient.
Moments like these—big and small—point to something deeper. It’s almost as if there’s a sense of right and wrong running through us that goes beyond just our culture or upbringing.
Most of us don’t stop to think about how often we use words like “fair,” “cruel,” “just,” or “wrong.” They just slip into our conversations, as if everyone knows what they mean. But in a world where people disagree about what’s right, the whole idea of morality can feel shaky. Some say right and wrong are just things we pick up from society or evolution—nothing more than habits and conventions. Others believe there’s got to be something more solid underneath it all.
Picture a philosophy student, reading about the darkest chapters of history. She just can’t accept that morality is only a matter of opinion. Deep down, she feels that things like kindness, honesty, and justice are good in themselves—not just because someone says so. Meanwhile, her friend, frustrated by the failures of religious institutions, wonders if it’s even possible to have real morality without God.
Here’s something to pay attention to: without some kind of ultimate standard, moral values start to lose their force. If right and wrong are just personal preferences, why bother standing up for justice? Why should we care about someone else’s suffering? But if morality is real—if some things are truly good or evil—then there must be something beyond just individuals or cultures that gives those values their weight.
And that brings us to meaning. The search for meaning is closely tied to morality. We want to know our lives matter, that our choices count, that love and sacrifice aren’t just illusions. In a world that can seem random and indifferent, this longing for purpose is a clue that maybe, just maybe, we’re made for more than just getting by.
Think about a teacher, reflecting on what she’s meant to her students. She realizes the most important things in life can’t be measured or bought. Love, courage, hope—they’re not just nice extras. They’re essential. And she starts to wonder if the foundation for these values goes deeper than anything the world can offer.
So, what’s the real journey here? It’s not just about signing up for a list of beliefs. It’s about discovering a story that actually makes sense of the world—a story where morality, meaning, and hope aren’t just wishful thinking, but signs pointing to something real. Something beautiful. Something true.
